Let's consider what each of these levels would need to look like for UML.
Splitting a straightforward method into a new class appears simple enough in programming, but should we even do it? It doesn't appear necessary to be able to perform such a refactoring operation in a UML class diagram.
Nevertheless, there is indeed a necessity to perform "preverbs" at the requirements level—particularly "distill requirements into preconditions," "optimize constraints on preconditions," and so forth, all the way through to three levels of refinement; from adding tables ('Observe') to establishing elements ('Preorder'), it appears quite sound.
These requirements shouldn't specify atomic preconditions that need to be checked honestly, but should instead flow within a context diagram's "effect chain." However, this misses the main point, which is that these preconditions are integral to UML, and thus refining them into code is quite straightforward.
There are many refactorings at the analysis level that aren't worth advancing to the programming level, as pushing Requirements Driven Development further could distort or negate its intent entirely. Modifying a traceability matrix, for instance, would basically mean: "I'm satisfied with the user, but now I need to set up a portal" and vice versa.
"Extract UI elements into classes" is very much one-for-one. In a UML "Deployment and Testing" diagram, an element named "graphical user interface" will represent a window (if we wish to model the abstract view through windows instead of screen shots), and a window is an object that "administrators" (referred to as high-level actors) interact with during Scrum and other development methodologies that are modeling-friendly.
